summary:
Five Nights At Mars is an educational survival game designed for children aged 7–12. Developed in Godot, it places players in the role of an astronaut responsible for maintaining a Martian habitat. Players manage limited resources, respond to equipment failures, and complete interactive minigames involving solar panel cleaning, electrical repairs, and water pumping.

The project addresses the challenge of making space exploration and engineering concepts accessible to younger audiences. Through simplified systems and observable consequences, players explore how energy, water, life support, and food production contribute to survival. Limited time and resources encourage them to prioritize tasks and consider how a failure in one system can affect others.

The project aims to turn abstract concepts into approachable, hands-on experiences. By combining exploration, problem-solving, and resource management, Five Nights At Mars seeks to spark curiosity about STEM and help children understand the engineering challenges of sustaining human life beyond Earth.

Five Nights At Mars

An Educational Mars Survival and Engineering Simulation

Abstract

Five Nights At Mars is an educational video game designed to introduce children to the challenges of human survival on Mars through an interactive astronaut survival simulation. The project aims to make space exploration and engineering concepts more accessible to younger audiences by allowing players to experience the responsibilities involved in maintaining a functional Martian habitat.

Players take on the role of an astronaut living on a Mars base, where they must monitor and maintain essential systems such as power generation, life support, water management, and food production. Throughout the game, different technical malfunctions and system failures challenge players to identify problems and restore the functionality of the habitat.

Each maintenance task is presented as an interactive minigame based on the malfunctioning system. These activities are designed around realistic engineering principles and scientifically grounded solutions, encouraging players to develop problem-solving skills, logical thinking, and an understanding of how interconnected systems support human life in an extreme environment.

By combining gameplay with simplified representations of real aerospace engineering challenges, Five Nights At Mars seeks to transform complex scientific concepts into engaging learning experiences. Ultimately, the project aims to inspire curiosity about space exploration and introduce younger generations to the importance of science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM).

Problem Statement

Space exploration involves complex engineering systems that must work together to support human life in extreme environments. A human habitat on Mars would depend on several interconnected systems, including power generation, life support, water management, and food production. Understanding how these systems operate, depend on one another, and respond to technical failures is essential to understanding the challenges of establishing a sustainable human presence on Mars.

However, these concepts can be difficult for children aged 7–12 to understand because they involve technical processes that are often invisible, abstract, or beyond their everyday experiences. Learning about space exploration through theoretical explanations alone may not provide enough opportunities for children to explore how engineering systems work or how real-world problems are approached and solved.

The challenge addressed by this project is the need for an engaging, age-appropriate educational experience that introduces children to the engineering principles behind human survival on Mars. Young learners should have the opportunity to understand not only what systems are necessary for a Mars habitat, but also why they are necessary, how they interact, and what happens when they stop functioning correctly.

To address this challenge, Five Nights At Mars proposes an interactive survival simulation in which players take the role of an astronaut responsible for maintaining a Martian habitat. Through gameplay and scenario-based maintenance minigames, players encounter simulated technical malfunctions, investigate their causes, and apply simplified solutions based on realistic engineering principles.

The project seeks to transform complex aerospace engineering concepts into accessible, hands-on learning experiences that encourage curiosity, critical thinking, and early interest in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM).

Objectives

To develop an engaging and entertaining educational video game for children aged 7–12 that introduces them to the engineering systems required to sustain human life on Mars. The project aims to spark curiosity and interest in engineering, science, and space exploration by allowing players to experience the challenges of maintaining a Martian habitat through interactive gameplay and realistic problem-solving scenarios.

 Specific Objectives

  • Introduce Engineering Systems: Help children understand the basic functions of essential Mars habitat systems, including power generation, life support, water management, and food production.
  • Encourage Problem-Solving Skills: Challenge players to identify technical malfunctions, investigate their causes, and apply appropriate solutions through interactive maintenance minigames.
  • Promote Scientific Understanding: Present simplified but scientifically grounded explanations of the processes and technologies involved in sustaining human life on Mars.
  • Inspire Interest in STEM: Encourage curiosity about engineering, technology, science, and space exploration by allowing children to interact with engineering challenges in an accessible environment.
  • Create an Enjoyable Learning Experience: Provide fun, interactive, and age-appropriate gameplay that combines entertainment with educational content, making learning an enjoyable part of the experience.
  • Demonstrate System Interdependence: Help players understand how different habitat systems depend on one another and how a malfunction in one system can affect the entire Mars base.
Proposed Solution

Five Nights At Mars is an educational survival and exploration video game in which players take the role of an astronaut stationed at a human habitat on Mars. The game combines resource management, engineering problem-solving, base maintenance, and planetary exploration to create an interactive learning experience for children aged 7–12.

The main objective of the gameplay is to maintain the functionality of the Martian habitat and survive for as long as possible while managing limited resources and investigating the surrounding environment of Mars.

The gameplay revolves around the continuous management and maintenance of the Mars base. Players must monitor essential resources such as electricity, water, oxygen, and food to ensure that the habitat remains operational. Each resource is connected to specific systems within the base, meaning that a malfunction in one station can affect the performance of other systems.

Throughout the game, different technical or environmental malfunctions may occur in the habitat. Players must identify the affected station, investigate the problem, and complete an interactive maintenance minigame to restore its functionality. These minigames are designed around realistic engineering concepts and simplified repair procedures, allowing players to understand the cause of a problem and the principles behind its solution.

The project uses interactive learning to introduce engineering and scientific concepts in an accessible and entertaining way. Rather than relying exclusively on written explanations, the game encourages players to learn by interacting with systems, identifying problems, and completing practical challenges.


Methodology

The development of Five Nights At Mars follows an iterative approach to design, implementation, and evaluation. Each cycle allows new features to be added, their behavior to be tested, and adjustments to be made before they are integrated into the overall game.

1. Content Design and Adaptation

The educational objectives are translated into interaction requirements and criteria for designing the challenges. Selected concepts are adapted into brief activities with clear instructions and observable outcomes. The proposed approach includes documenting the scientific sources consulted and distinguishing educational simplifications from parameters chosen to balance gameplay.

2. Prototype Development and Integration

The prototype is implemented in Godot using GDScript, independent scenes, and reusable components. Separating logic from presentation allows visual and functional elements to be developed and adjusted independently.

Each minigame is integrated with the overall task, resource, and event management systems. Modular development allows each component to be tested separately before verifying its behavior within a complete gameplay session.

3. Technical Verification and Refinement

Functional tests are conducted to verify task initiation, completion, and cancellation, as well as resource updates and event resolution. Testing also checks that integration does not cause duplicate actions or incorrect changes to game time.

Identified errors are corrected, and the affected scenarios are tested again. This process allows the prototype’s stability to be assessed progressively.

4. User Evaluation

As a subsequent stage, the project proposes testing with participants from the target audience, with permission from their parents or guardians. The evaluation will observe their understanding of instructions, task completion, and need for assistance.

The evaluation may be supplemented with brief questions before and after gameplay to explore participants’ understanding of the concepts presented. The results will guide adjustments to difficulty, the interface, and educational content.


System architecture

The Mars habitat is designed as an interconnected network of essential systems that work together to sustain the astronaut and maintain the functionality of the base. Each station performs a specific task, but its operation depends on the availability of resources and the functionality of other stations.

The architecture is built around two central resources: electricity and water. The Power Station acts as the primary source of electrical energy, while the Water Station manages water recovery, treatment, storage, and distribution. These resources are supplied to the other stations according to their operational requirements.

The four primary stations are:

  • Power Station: Generates electricity through solar panels and stores excess energy in batteries. It distributes electricity to all other stations.
  • Life Support Station: Maintains suitable atmospheric conditions inside the habitat, including oxygen supply, air circulation, and carbon dioxide removal. It requires electricity and processed water for its oxygen generation system.
  • Water Station: Processes and recovers water, maintaining storage reserves and distributing clean water to the astronaut and other systems.
  • Greenhouse: Produces food using controlled environmental conditions. It requires electricity for lighting and environmental control, as well as water and nutrients for plant growth.

The architecture also considers resource storage as a way to prevent an immediate shutdown when a station experiences a malfunction. Energy, Food and water reservoirs provide temporary reserves, allowing the player to respond to emergencies before the consequences become critical.

The stations are interconnected through resource distribution and operational dependencies. This means that a failure in one station may affect the functionality of multiple systems.

Power Dependencies

The Power Station distributes electricity throughout the habitat. The Life Support, Water Station, and Greenhouse all require electrical power to operate their main equipment.

If electricity generation decreases, the base begins consuming energy stored in its batteries. If the energy reserves become insufficient, the player must prioritize which systems receive electricity to maintain the most important functions.

Water Dependencies

The Water Station provides treated water for the astronaut, the Life Support Station, and the Greenhouse.

The Life Support Station uses water as part of its oxygen generation process, while the Greenhouse requires water for irrigation and plant development. A failure in water processing or distribution can therefore affect both breathable oxygen production and food production.

Life Support Dependencies

Life Support depends on a continuous supply of electricity to operate ventilation, atmospheric monitoring, filtration, and oxygen generation equipment.

Its operation is essential for maintaining a habitable environment. A failure in this station represents a direct threat to the astronaut and should generally receive the highest repair priority.

Greenhouse Dependencies

The Greenhouse depends on electricity and water to maintain its growing environment. Its main contribution to the habitat is food production.

Although the Greenhouse may support biological research and contribute to atmospheric studies, it is not considered the primary source of breathable oxygen. Its failure mainly affects long-term food availability.

Priorities

An important gameplay mechanic is the ability to assign priorities to maintenance tasks. Since the player has limited time and resources, it is not always possible or necessary to repair every malfunction immediately.

Instead of automatically repairing the first station that develops a problem, the player must evaluate the situation and determine which repair will provide the greatest benefit to the survival of the habitat.

To support this decision-making process, each malfunction presents information that helps the player evaluate its importance:

  • How serious is the malfunction?
  • Which resources are being lost or affected?
  • How many other stations depend on the affected system?
  • How much mission time is required to complete the repair?
  • What could happen if the player postpones the repair?

Based on this information, the player assigns a priority level to each maintenance task.

The proposed priority levels are:

Critical Priority: Malfunctions that directly threaten the astronaut's survival or disable essential habitat functions. These repairs should be addressed immediately.

High Priority: Malfunctions that significantly reduce essential resource availability or affect multiple interconnected systems. They may not cause immediate danger, but delaying repairs can create a larger problem.

Medium Priority: Malfunctions that reduce operational efficiency or affect long-term resource production, but do not immediately threaten the astronaut.

Low Priority: Minor malfunctions that have limited consequences or affect systems with sufficient backup resources. These repairs can be postponed until more urgent tasks are completed.

The interconnected system architecture is designed to demonstrate that engineering systems do not operate independently. Their functionality depends on the availability of resources, proper maintenance, and the coordination of different components.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"" ]Conclusión

Five Nights At Mars has established a playable foundation for an educational Mars-habitat survival simulation. The project combines base resource management, four essential stations, rover sample discoveries, and maintenance challenges that turn engineering problems into concrete player actions. The evidence in this report presents the title and end-of-day interfaces alongside standalone examples for electrical repair, solar cleaning, air-leak repair, and frozen-pipe repair. 

The current build remains a prototype. The next development stage should connect station malfunctions to their minigames, complete the intended startup flow, resolve the cleanup warnings, and evaluate usability and learning with the target age group. These steps would build on the working mechanics to deliver an integrated, testable STEM learning experience.
